payroll_function.title: Payroll 1 — The Payroll Function & Salary Structures
payroll_function.desc: The pay machinery in ZhiftERP: the seven-step pipeline and the custody split; the Employee record's payroll fields (Salary Mode, bank details under custody rules, Payroll Cost Center, Holiday List); the Salary Component's flags and Accounts table; the Salary Structure as the package template with the B/H/T split; the Salary Structure Assignment carrying the Base, From Date, and Income Tax Slab link with the supersession rule; formulas, conditions, and payment-days proration; and the preview procedure with its five reads.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The pay pipeline in ZhiftERP
lessons.html:
This track certifies the payroll operator in ZhiftERP. This module covers the machinery that computes pay: the Employee record's payroll fields, Salary Components, the Salary Structure, the Salary Structure Assignment, formulas and payment days, and the preview procedure that verifies a structure before it pays anyone.

The pipeline. Pay in ZhiftERP is computed by a chain of records. Learn the chain in order, because every module of this track works somewhere on it:

1. Employee — the person, with the payroll fields Chapter 2 walks.
2. Salary Component — one pay element: Basic, Housing, PAYE, Pension. Each component carries its type, its calculation, and its ledger account (Chapter 3).
3. Salary Structure — a named template listing which components make up a pay package (Chapter 4).
4. Salary Structure Assignment — the record that attaches a structure to one employee from a date, with that employee's base amount (Chapter 5).
5. Payroll Entry — the monthly run: selects the employees, generates their slips (module 3).
6. Salary Slip — one employee's computed pay for one period: earnings, deductions, net (modules 3-4).
7. The posting and the payment — the accrual Journal Entry the run books, and the bank payment (modules 2-3).

The design consequence. Because pay is computed by this chain, the operator's work is maintaining records, not calculating amounts: when the structure is right, every slip is right; when a slip is wrong, the fault is in a record — a component's formula, an assignment's base, an employee's field — and the fix is made there, once, for every future month. A payroll kept in a spreadsheet beside the system has none of this: every month is recomputed by hand, every error is repeated until noticed, and the accounts, tax, and audit machinery downstream receives nothing.

The custody split. Three owners share the payroll function, and the split is held throughout the track:

• HR owns who is employed, on what terms, from when — the Employee records and the approved pay decisions.
• The payroll operator (this certification) owns the machinery: components, structures, assignments, the run, the slips, the registers.
• The accountant owns the numbers' policy: the tax table, the statutory rates, the account wiring — module 2's territory.

Module contents. Chapter 2: the Employee record's payroll fields. Chapter 3: Salary Components. Chapter 4: the Salary Structure. Chapter 5: the Salary Structure Assignment. Chapter 6: formulas, conditions, and payment days. Chapter 7: the preview procedure. Chapter 8: the HealthTrade case. Chapter 9: review and the law.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The Employee record: the payroll fields
lessons.html:
Open an Employee record (awesome bar → Employee). HR owns the record; the payroll operator verifies the fields the pay machinery reads. Walk them in order.

1. Company. The employing entity. On a multi-company site, the employee's slips, postings, and registers all belong to this company — the legal-separation rule reaching payroll.

2. Date of Joining. The first month's proration reads this date (Chapter 6). A wrong joining date pays a wrong first month.

3. Status and Relieving Date. Status Active means the run picks the employee up; Left with a Relieving Date means the final month prorates to that date and later runs exclude them (module 7 covers exits in full). The run selects by these fields — an exit not recorded here is a leaver who keeps getting paid.

4. Salary Mode, and the bank fields. Salary Mode = Bank, Cash, or Cheque. For Bank: the Bank Name and Bank A/C No. fields feed the payment run. Rules:

• Bank details are entered from the employee's own written instruction, filed as an attachment on the record.
• Changes to bank details are governed master-data events — verified with the employee through a known channel, never actioned from a forwarded message. This is the same rule the Accounts track applies to supplier bank details, for the same fraud.

5. Payroll Cost Center. The address the employee's salary cost posts to — the branch or unit. Set per employee (or defaulted from the Department where the site is configured so). This one field is what makes the branch P&L's salary line true; an employee without it posts into the company fallback and distorts every branch read.

6. Holiday List. The employee's working calendar. Payment-days proration (Chapter 6) counts working days from this list; leave machinery (the HR track) shares it. Confirm every employee carries the correct list — the branch that works Saturdays needs its own.

7. The tax and statutory fields. The state of residence (module 2's PAYE split reads it), the pension fund administrator and PFA account number (module 2's remittance schedule reads them), and the tax identifiers. Module 2 walks each at its station.

The verification procedure. Before any employee's first run:

1. Open the Employee record.
2. Confirm fields 1-7 against the offer letter and the employee's forms.
3. Attach the source documents to the record.
4. Note the verification in the record's comments: date, by whom.

Practical rule: the run inherits every error this walk would have caught. Five minutes per joiner; module 3's checklist assumes it was done.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — The Salary Component
lessons.html:
Open Salary Component (awesome bar) > New. One component is one pay element, and its fields decide how it computes, how it taxes, and where it posts. Walk the fields.

1. Name and Abbreviation. The name prints on every payslip (write it as the employee should read it: Housing Allowance, not HRA2). The abbreviation is the handle formulas use (Chapter 6): Basic's abbreviation B lets another component compute B * 0.1. Set abbreviations short and stable; changing one later breaks every formula that references it.

2. Type: Earning or Deduction. Earnings add to gross; deductions subtract toward net. The statutory deductions (module 2) are Deduction-type components.

3. The calculation block. Either a fixed Amount, or Amount based on formula with the Formula field (Chapter 6 teaches the writing), plus an optional Condition that must be true for the component to apply at all. A component with neither amount nor formula takes its value from the Salary Structure's row (Chapter 4) — the per-structure override pattern.

4. Is Tax Applicable. Ticked, the component's amount counts toward taxable income; clear, it is exempt. This flag is set per component from the accountant's ruling — which allowances are taxable is tax policy, not operator preference, and the 2025 reform's changes land exactly here at the annual re-read (module 2).

5. Depends on Payment Days. Ticked, the component prorates with the month's payable days — the joiner from the 16th earns roughly half; unpaid leave reduces it (Chapter 6's mechanics). Clear, the component pays flat regardless. Salary-like earnings tick it; fixed reimbursements usually do not.

6. Do Not Include in Total / Statistical Component. Two visibility controls: a Statistical Component computes but pays nothing — used as a base figure other formulas reference; Do Not Include in Total shows a line without moving net pay — module 2 uses it for the employer pension share, which the employee should see but does not pay.

7. The Accounts table. One row per company: the component's ledger account. Earnings point at their expense accounts (Salary expense, split by component family where the chart wants it); statutory deductions point at their custody accounts — PAYE Payable, Pension Payable (module 2 wires each). This table is where payroll meets the Accounts track: the run's accrual Journal Entry posts every component to the account named here, addressed by the employee's Payroll Cost Center. A component with a missing or wrong account row mis-posts every month for every employee that carries it.

The component register. Keep the one-page list: every component with its type, flags, formula, account, and the ruling that set Is Tax Applicable. Reviewed at module 8's annual walk; every new component is a governed addition to this page, not a keyboard improvisation.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — The Salary Structure
lessons.html:
Open Salary Structure (awesome bar) > New. A structure is a named pay-package template: which components, in which arrangement, for one family of employees. Walk the form.

1. Name and Company. Name structures for the package, not the person: Head Office Staff, Branch Retail Staff, Management. One structure serves every employee on that package; a structure per person is Chapter 9's Pattern 2.

2. Payroll Frequency. Monthly for the standard Nigerian salary cycle. The frequency governs the run's periods.

3. The Earnings table. One row per earning component. Each row carries the component and — where the component itself has no formula — the row-level amount or formula. The standard Nigerian shape enters here as component rows computed from the base (Chapter 5's assignment supplies the base):

• Basic — commonly a percentage of the base (formula on the assignment's base).
• Housing and Transport — percentages likewise. The Basic + Housing + Transport family matters beyond presentation: module 2's pension computes on it, so the split is the accountant's decision, recorded.
• The remaining allowances per the package — each an existing component from Chapter 3's register.

4. The Deductions table. The deduction components this package carries: the statutory set (PAYE, employee pension, NHF where applicable — module 2 builds each) plus any package-specific deductions. Because the statutory components carry their own formulas and flags, the structure usually just lists them — the computation lives on the component, the membership lives on the structure.

5. The payment and posting defaults. The structure carries the Mode of Payment and payment-account defaults the run will use, plus leave-encashment settings where the leave policy uses them (the HR track's territory; noted here for the field walk).

6. Submit. Structures are submittable documents: submitted, they can be assigned; amendments follow the document rules — a change to a live structure is a governed event (module 6 covers pay changes properly; module 8 covers structure versioning).

The design procedure.

1. List the pay packages that actually exist — usually three to six families, not one per person.
2. Confirm the component set and the B/H/T split per package with the accountant.
3. Build each structure from registered components only.
4. Preview one slip per structure (Chapter 7) before any assignment goes live.

Practical rule: the structure count is a health number. Three structures for thirty staff is a design; twenty-eight structures for thirty staff is a spreadsheet wearing a costume of records — merge them by package and carry the differences on the assignment's base.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — The Salary Structure Assignment
lessons.html:
Open Salary Structure Assignment (awesome bar) > New. The assignment is the record that joins one employee to one structure from one date, and carries the number the formulas compute from. Walk the fields.

1. Employee and Salary Structure. The person and the package template. One employee has one active assignment at a time; a new assignment from a later date supersedes the old from that date — which is exactly how pay rises are recorded (module 6): not by editing history, but by a new assignment from the effective date.

2. From Date. When this assignment starts governing. Rules:

• The first assignment's From Date aligns with the Date of Joining (or the pay decision's effective date).
• From Dates are honest dates. A rise effective the 1st is dated the 1st, even if entered on the 20th — the run computes from the record, and module 3's run for that month will apply it correctly.

3. Base. The assignment's central field: the employee's base amount, from which the structure's percentage formulas compute. The base is the pay decision, as a number — it comes from the offer letter or the approved review (module 6), it is entered once here, and every component that says base * something reads it. Two employees on the same structure with different bases produce different slips from one template: this is how three structures serve thirty staff.

4. Variable. The second reference amount, available to formulas as the variable-pay anchor where the package uses one (module 5's territory).

5. Income Tax Slab. The assignment links the employee to the Income Tax Slab that computes their PAYE — module 2, Chapter 2 builds the slab; this field is where it attaches. An assignment without its slab produces a slip without its tax: the preview (Chapter 7) checks for exactly this.

6. Company and Currency. Per the employee's record; the naira for this track's scope.

The assignment procedures.

• The joiner: Employee verified (Chapter 2) → assignment created with structure, From Date, Base from the offer letter, slab attached → preview (Chapter 7) → filed.
• The pay change: new assignment from the effective date with the new base; the old assignment stands as history. Never edit an old assignment's base — that rewrites what past months were computed from, and the register stops matching the slips it produced.
• The bulk load at go-live: assignments imported through the Data Import tool under the sysadmin track's six-step governed procedure, then every structure previewed and a sample of individual slips checked against the old payroll's last month.

Practical rule: the assignment list, filtered by structure, is the answer to "who is on what package at what base" — the pay register in one view. Module 6's governance reads it; keep it clean.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Formulas, conditions, and payment days
lessons.html:
The computation layer. Three mechanics, each with its procedure.

Formulas. A component's Formula field computes its amount each run. The writing rules:

1. Reference by abbreviation and by base. base * 0.4 computes forty percent of the assignment's Base. B * 0.1 computes ten percent of the component whose abbreviation is B — component-on-component references, which is how pension computes on Basic + Housing + Transport: (B + H + T) * 0.08 (module 2 builds it).
2. Order matters through dependency: a formula can only reference components that compute before it. Keep the dependency shallow — base-referencing formulas for the earnings, family-sum formulas for the statutory set — and the evaluation stays readable.
3. Write the formula on the component when it is universal (pension's rate is law, the same everywhere) and on the structure's row when it is per-package (Basic's percentage differs by package). One home per formula; a formula duplicated in both places is a future contradiction.

Conditions. The Condition field gates whether the component applies at all: a component conditioned on base > 0 always applies; one conditioned on a field or threshold applies selectively (module 2 uses a condition where a levy applies only above a threshold; module 5 uses them for variable pay). The rule: conditions encode written policy — every condition traces to a line on the policy page, because a condition nobody can explain is a deduction nobody can defend.

Payment days — the proration engine. For components with Depends on Payment Days ticked, the slip computes: payment days = working days in the period (from the employee's Holiday List) − unmarked absences and leave without pay (from the leave machinery), and the component pays amount × payment days ÷ working days. The three standing cases:

• The mid-month joiner: Date of Joining on the 16th → payment days run from the 16th → the salary-like components pay their fraction automatically. No manual arithmetic; the record computed it.
• The mid-month leaver: Relieving Date the 12th → the final slip prorates to the 12th (module 7 completes the exit).
• Leave without pay: approved LWP days reduce payment days — the HR track's leave records feeding this track's slips. The operator's check: the slip's payment-days figure against the month's known absences, per module 3's run checklist.

The verification habit. Every formula, condition, and proration rule is verified the same way: one previewed slip (Chapter 7) whose arithmetic is checked by hand once. After that single hand-check, the record computes every future month — which is the pipeline's whole promise, and why the hand-check is never skipped on the first pass.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The preview procedure
lessons.html:
No structure pays anyone before a previewed slip has been read against the source documents. This chapter is that procedure — the track's equivalent of the Accounts track's posting-map verification.

Previewing one slip.

1. Open Salary Slip (awesome bar) > New.
2. Select the Employee and the payroll period. The form pulls the employee's active assignment, its structure, and its slab, and computes: every earning row, every deduction row, the payment days, gross, total deductions, net.
3. Do not submit. The preview is read and discarded (or saved as draft and deleted after) — module 3's run generates the real slips. The preview exists to be checked, not to pay.

The reading, line by line.

1. Earnings against the offer letter: each component present, each amount matching the letter's package arithmetic. The Basic/Housing/Transport split at the agreed percentages of the base.
2. Deductions against the accountant's table: PAYE present and plausible against the slab (module 2's Chapter 2 gives the plausibility check), pension at its rate on the right family, the other statutory lines per applicability.
3. Payment days against the calendar: full month = full days; the joiner's fraction correct.
4. Net pay stated back: gross − deductions = net, and the net against what the employee was told they would receive. A package quoted net in the offer letter is reconciled to its gross here — before the first payday conversation, not during it.
5. One hand-check: one formula-computed line recomputed manually (Chapter 6's rule). One line suffices; it proves the chain.

When to preview.

• Every new structure, before its first assignment — one preview per structure at a representative base.
• Every joiner, at assignment — their own preview against their own letter.
• Every pay change — the new assignment previewed before its first run.
• Every component or formula change — one preview per affected structure (module 8's change discipline; the sysadmin track's test-then-live logic applied to pay).
• After the go-live bulk load — every structure, plus a sample of individuals against the old payroll's last month.

The record. Each preview gets one line in the payroll log: employee/structure, date, checked against what, by whom, result. Findings are fixed in the records (the component, the row, the assignment) and re-previewed — never patched on the slip, because a slip patch fixes one month and leaves the record wrong for every month after.

Practical rule: the preview costs five minutes and runs before money moves; the same error found on payday costs a correction run, a bank recall attempt, and an employee's trust. Every module downstream assumes the preview happened.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Case study: HealthTrade's structures
lessons.html:
HealthTrade builds its pay machinery. Every chapter appears. (HealthTrade is the pharmaceutical distributor the whole programme follows — three branches, Head Office, about thirty staff.)

Step 1 — the employee walk (Chapter 2). All employee records are verified against files: two records carry no Payroll Cost Center (their salary cost had been landing in the company fallback — the Accounts track's unaddressed check had already flagged the naira; this walk names the cause), one bank account number fails its verification and is corrected from the employee's written instruction, and every record gets its Holiday List confirmed — the retail branches on the Saturdays-working list, Head Office on the standard list.

Step 2 — the component register (Chapter 3). Built with the accountant in one sitting: the earnings set (Basic, Housing, Transport, plus a Meal and a Utility allowance) with Is Tax Applicable ruled per line and the accounts table pointed at the salary expense accounts; the deduction set left as stubs for module 2's statutory build. Abbreviations set short (B, H, T) because the pension formula will reference them. The register page is written: every component, its flags, its account, its ruling.

Step 3 — the structures (Chapter 4). The package census finds three families, not thirty: Branch Retail Staff, Head Office Staff, Management. Three Salary Structures are built, the B/H/T split confirmed with the accountant (recorded: the split feeds pension), the earnings rows carrying per-package percentages of base, the deduction membership listed.

Step 4 — the assignments (Chapter 5). Thirty Salary Structure Assignments load through the governed import: employee, structure, From Date, Base from each offer letter. The assignment list filtered by structure becomes the standing pay register — who is on what package at what base, one view.

Step 5 — the previews (Chapters 6-7). One preview per structure at a representative base, then a five-employee sample against the old spreadsheet payroll's last month. The previews catch two findings before anyone is paid: a Transport formula on the Retail structure written as base * 0.15 where the letter said ten percent — a typing error that would have overpaid eleven staff monthly — and one mid-2025 joiner whose old spreadsheet had never prorated the first month (the spreadsheet had paid the full month; the slip's payment-days figure computes the truth, and the difference is documented for the file rather than clawed back — the owner's call, recorded). Both fixes land in the records — the structure row corrected, re-previewed, logged.

The state at module's end. Three structures, thirty verified assignments, a component register with rulings, and a preview log with two findings closed. The statutory deductions are stubs awaiting module 2 — which is exactly where the track goes next. The payroll operator's note in the log: the spreadsheet computed pay thirty times a month; the records now compute it once, per rule.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Common mistakes & the first law
lessons.html:
The structure layer's recurring failures, then the review list.

Pattern 1 — the spreadsheet beside the system. Symptom: pay computed in a spreadsheet, one lump posted monthly; no slips, no register, no proration, no audit trail; every downstream module starved. Cause: the pipeline never built (Chapter 1). Fix: this module, run in order — the employee walk, the component register, the structures, the assignments, the previews — with the sample-against-last-month check making the cutover safe.

Pattern 2 — the structure per person. Symptom: as many structures as staff; every pay change a structure edit; no package view. Cause: the base misunderstood — differences that belong on the assignment's Base built as separate templates (Chapters 4-5). Fix: the package census, structures merged to the real families, differences moved to bases, and the structure count watched as a health number.

Pattern 3 — the edited history. Symptom: pay rises made by editing the old assignment's base; the register no longer matching the slips it produced; last year's figures silently different. Cause: the supersession rule unknown (Chapter 5). Fix: new assignment from the effective date, always; old assignments as history, never edited; module 6's governance making the rule structural.

Pattern 4 — the unverified formula. Symptom: a percentage typed wrong paying every carrier of the structure wrong, monthly, until an employee complains. Cause: the preview skipped (Chapters 6-7). Fix: the preview procedure at every trigger — new structure, joiner, change, go-live — with its one hand-check and its log line.

Pattern 5 — the unaddressed salary. Symptom: the branch P&L's salary line untrue; payroll cost pooled in the company fallback. Cause: Payroll Cost Center blank on employee records (Chapter 2). Fix: the field on the joiner checklist, the existing records swept, and the Accounts track's monthly unaddressed check standing guard.

Pattern 6 — the slip patch. Symptom: errors "fixed" by editing the month's slip; the same error returning next month; records and slips diverging. Cause: fixes made downstream of the fault (Chapter 7). Fix: the rule — findings are fixed in the records and re-previewed; the slip is output, never the place of repair.

The review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: recite the seven-step pipeline and the custody split; walk the Employee record's seven payroll fields and run the joiner verification; create a Salary Component and explain each flag — Is Tax Applicable, Depends on Payment Days, Statistical, Do Not Include in Total — and the Accounts table; build a Salary Structure with its earnings and deductions tables and defend the structure count; create a Salary Structure Assignment with Base, From Date, and the slab link, and state the supersession rule; write a base formula and a component-family formula, and compute a joiner's payment days; and run the preview procedure with its five reads and its log line.

The first law: pay is computed by the records — components carry their accounts, structures carry the package, assignments carry the base, and every slip previews before it pays. Module 2 builds the statutory deductions: PAYE, pension, and the Nigerian compliance set.

statutory.title: Payroll 2 — Statutory Deductions & Nigerian Compliance
statutory.desc: The statutory layer in ZhiftERP: the custody frame and the division of authority; the Income Tax Slab built from the accountant's table with the PAYE component's taxable-salary flag and the plausibility check; pension's two shares on the B/H/T family with per-PFA schedules; NHF and the levies from the applicability register; the state-of-residence PAYE split; account wiring proven by the posting read and the monthly payroll tie; the six-step remittance workflow with the zero check; and the Salary Register — one monthly record, derived schedules, confidentiality enforced.

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — The statutory layer: custody components
lessons.html:
This module builds the statutory deductions in ZhiftERP: the Income Tax Slab and PAYE, pension, NHF and the levy family, the state-of-residence split, the account wiring and the posting read, the remittance workflow, and the Salary Register report.

The custody frame, carried in. The Accounts track's fifth law governs this module from the other side: amounts withheld from the employee — PAYE, the employee pension share, NHF — are custody money, held for an authority, and amounts borne by the employer — the employer pension share, NSITF, ITF — are the business's own cost. In the machinery, both are Salary Components; the difference is carried by the component's type and flags, and by which account its Accounts table names:

• Employee-withheld amounts: Deduction-type components, posting to custody accounts (PAYE Payable, Pension Payable, NHF Payable — Tax-type leaves the Accounts track created).
• Employer-borne amounts: components that show without reducing net (Chapter 3's mechanics), posting expense against the matching payable.

The division of authority, stated for this module. The rates, bands, reliefs, thresholds, and applicability rules are the accountant's table — statute, read from current law, re-read annually and at every reform. The 2025 tax reform re-shaped the personal income tax structure; this manual therefore teaches no rates as facts. It teaches the machinery: where the accountant's numbers are entered, how the components compute from them, and how the results are proven. The operator's competence is the machinery; the operator's discipline is refusing to improvise a rate.

The statutory set, previewed. The components this module builds, each at its chapter:

1. PAYE — the income tax deduction, computed by the Income Tax Slab (Chapter 2).
2. Pension — employee and employer shares on the B/H/T family (Chapter 3).
3. NHF, NSITF, ITF — the housing fund and the employer levies, per applicability (Chapter 4).
4. The state split for PAYE remittance (Chapter 5).

Module contents. Chapter 2: the Income Tax Slab and the PAYE component. Chapter 3: pension. Chapter 4: NHF and the levies. Chapter 5: the state-of-residence split. Chapter 6: account wiring and the posting read. Chapter 7: the remittance workflow. Chapter 8: the Salary Register. Chapter 9: the HealthTrade case. Chapter 10: review and the law.

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The Income Tax Slab and the PAYE component
lessons.html:
PAYE in ZhiftERP is computed by two records working together: the Income Tax Slab (the accountant's table, entered once) and the PAYE Salary Component (the deduction that applies it). Build them in that order.

Building the Income Tax Slab.

1. Open Income Tax Slab (awesome bar) > New.
2. Name it for its source and effective date — PAYE — [year] table — and set the Company, Currency, and Effective From date.
3. Enter the Standard Tax Exemption Amount where the current law's relief structure maps to one — the consolidated relief and exemption figures come from the accountant's current computation sheet, entered as the law states them at entry time.
4. Enter the slab rows: each row is an income band with its percentage — the graduated bands from the accountant's table, transcribed exactly. Conditions on rows serve where the law's structure needs them; the accountant reads the built slab against their table before it is used.
5. Submit. A new law or reform means a new slab with its own Effective From — never an edit to the old one, which computed history.

Building the PAYE component.

1. Open Salary Component > New: name PAYE, Type = Deduction.
2. Tick the component's income-tax flag (Variable Based On Taxable Salary) — this is what tells the run to compute the amount from the employee's slab and taxable income rather than from a formula.
3. Accounts table: the company row pointing at PAYE Payable (Chapter 6 verifies the posting).
4. Add the component to every structure's Deductions table (module 1, Chapter 4).

Attaching the slab. The slab links on each employee's Salary Structure Assignment (module 1, Chapter 5). The run then computes each employee's PAYE from: their taxable earnings (the components with Is Tax Applicable ticked — module 1's flag now doing its work), less the slab's exemptions, through the slab's bands, divided to the monthly figure.

The plausibility check — the operator's proof. For one previewed slip:

1. Sum the taxable earnings (the flagged components only).
2. Run the sum through the accountant's paper computation for one employee — the accountant's sheet is the reference, the slip is the candidate.
3. They must agree. Disagreement means a flag is wrong (a component taxable that should be exempt, or the reverse), a slab row mis-transcribed, or the exemption figure wrong — all record fixes, found on one slip before thirty slips inherit them.

Practical rule: the slab is re-read every year and at every reform announcement — the accountant confirms it still matches law, and a change produces a new dated slab attached by new assignments. The slab that quietly drifted from statute is a compliance failure computed automatically, thirty times a month.

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Pension: two shares, one family
lessons.html:
The contributory pension deducts an employee share and adds an employer share, both computed on the Basic + Housing + Transport family. The current statutory rates come from the accountant's table; the build is the same at any rates.

The employee share.

1. Salary Component > New: Pension — Employee, Type = Deduction.
2. Formula: (B + H + T) * [the employee rate] — the abbreviations module 1 set on Basic, Housing, and Transport now earning their keep. The rate figure is entered from the accountant's table and noted on the component register with its source.
3. Is Tax Applicable consequence: pension contributions carry tax treatment (deductible against taxable income under the law's rules) — the accountant rules how the slab's exemption structure and the component flags interact, and the Chapter 2 plausibility check proves the combination on one slip.
4. Accounts table: Pension Payable.

The employer share. The employer's contribution is the business's cost, not the employee's deduction — it must appear (the employee should see the full contribution going to their fund) without reducing net pay:

1. Salary Component > New: Pension — Employer, configured with the visibility flags from module 1 Chapter 3 — shown on the slip, excluded from the net computation (Do Not Include in Total), and computed by the same family formula at the employer rate.
2. Accounts: the employer share posts pension expense against Pension Payable — so the payable account accumulates both shares, which is the figure the remittance pays (Chapter 7).

The PFA dimension. Remittance is per employee, to each employee's own fund administrator. The machinery:

• The Employee record carries the PFA and the RSA (retirement savings account) number — module 1's Chapter 2 walk verified them; a joiner without a PFA is chased at joining, not at remittance.
• The remittance schedule (Chapter 7) is the month's pension figures split by PFA — the Salary Register's export grouped on the PFA field (Chapter 8), each PFA's schedule listing its employees with RSA numbers and both shares.

The timing rule, carried from the Accounts track. Pension remittance is pinned to days from paying salaries — the tightest window in the statutory family. The calendar line reads: salaries paid on the 25th → pension schedules and payments out within the statutory number of days, owned by name. Chapter 7 places it in the workflow.

Practical rule: the pension preview check is two multiplications — the family sum times each rate — done once by hand on one slip. The B/H/T split (module 1's recorded accountant decision) is what those multiplications stand on: a structure that quietly changed its split has changed every pension amount, which is why the split is a governed number.

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — NHF and the employer levies
lessons.html:
The remaining statutory family: one employee deduction and the employer levies. Each is a component built the same way; each begins with an applicability ruling from the accountant, because these obligations attach by headcount, sector, and election under the current law.

NHF — the housing fund.

1. The ruling first: whether NHF applies to this business's employees, and at what rate on what base (historically a percentage of Basic; the current position is the accountant's line). Where the law makes participation elective for some categories, the election is documented per employee, and the component's Condition field (module 1, Chapter 6) gates it accordingly.
2. Salary Component > New: NHF, Type = Deduction, Formula on the ruled base — B * [rate] — Accounts table pointing at NHF Payable.
3. Added to the structures whose staff it covers.

NSITF — the employees' compensation levy. Employer-borne: a percentage of payroll per the ruling.

1. Configured as an employer-cost component (the Chapter 3 employer pattern: visible or statistical per the business's slip-presentation choice, excluded from net) or — where the business prefers — computed off-slip by the accountant's monthly journal from the Salary Register's totals. Either home is lawful; one home is chosen and recorded, because a levy computed in both places pays twice.
2. Accounts: NSITF expense against NSITF Payable.

ITF — the training fund. Employer-borne, applicability by headcount/turnover thresholds per the ruling — the Condition field or the off-slip route, same one-home rule, posting to ITF Payable.

The applicability register. One page, kept with the component register: each statutory line, the ruling (applies / does not apply / applies to these categories), the rate and base, the ruling's source and date, and the component or journal that implements it. Two reads use this page:

1. The annual re-read — every ruling re-confirmed against current law with the accountant; the 2025 reform's consolidation makes this read the year's most important ten minutes.
2. The threshold watch — obligations that attach by headcount are re-checked when the business grows: the levy that did not apply at eleven staff may apply at twenty-six, and the applicability register is where that question lives instead of in nobody's memory.

Practical rule: a statutory component with no ruling behind it is an improvisation, whichever direction it errs — deducting what the law does not require injures the employee; skipping what it does require accrues penalties. The page-before-the-component order is absolute in this chapter.

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — The state-of-residence split
lessons.html:
PAYE remits to the state of each employee's residence — one business, several state authorities, one calendar. The machinery is one field, one grouping, and one discipline.

The field. The Employee record carries the residential address, and with it the state of residence — verified at joining from the employee's declared address (module 1's Chapter 2 walk), and updated as a governed event when the employee moves (the employee's written notice, filed on the record; the change effective from the notice for future remittances).

The grouping. The month's PAYE total is not one figure — it is a set of figures, one per state with resident employees. The mechanics:

1. The run computes each employee's PAYE (Chapter 2's machinery).
2. The Salary Register (Chapter 8) exports the month's slips with the employee dimension — grouped or pivoted on the state field, it produces the per-state schedule: each state's employees, their PAYE amounts, the state subtotal.
3. Each state's remittance (Chapter 7) pays its subtotal to that state's authority, with the schedule as the evidence behind the payment.

The standing example. A Lagos head office with Ogun-resident staff files in both states: Lagos receives the Lagos residents' PAYE, Ogun the Ogun residents' — the office's own location is not the test; the employees' residence is. A three-branch business spanning states multiplies the schedule accordingly, and the register's grouping produces all of it from the same run.

The discipline — why the field is governed. The state field is a remittance-routing field: wrong, it sends an employee's tax to the wrong authority, which surfaces later as the right authority's demand for tax "never received" plus the wrong authority's money to recover — two conversations, both slow. Hence:

1. The field is mandatory at joining — the verification walk refuses a blank.
2. Changes are evidenced — the employee's notice, filed.
3. The annual sweep — once a year, the state field列 is exported and each employee confirms their state in the same pass as the payslip-details confirmation (module 4's communication routines carry it) — catches the silent movers.

The registration prerequisite, flagged to the accountant. Remitting to a state requires the business to be registered with that state's authority. The operator's job is the flag: the first month a new state appears in the schedule (a new joiner resident somewhere new), the accountant is told before remittance day, because the registration is their process and it takes longer than a payment.

Practical rule: the per-state schedule is produced monthly even in the months it looks identical — the schedule is the remittance's evidence, and the month it changes silently (a mover, a joiner) is exactly the month a from-memory remittance goes wrong.

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — Account wiring and the posting read
lessons.html:
Every statutory component posts to the ledger through its Accounts table. This chapter wires the accounts and proves the posting — the Accounts track's posting-map verification, performed for payroll.

The wiring map. Confirm each component's Accounts table row (per company):

• Earnings components → the salary expense accounts (split by component family where the chart design wants Basic and allowances read separately).
• PAYE → PAYE Payable. Pension (both shares) → Pension Payable (the employer share's expense side to pension expense). NHF → NHF Payable. NSITF / ITF → their payables against their expenses.
• Every payable named here is a Tax-type custody leaf the Accounts track created — if one is missing from the chart, it is created there first (typed, named plainly), then wired here.

What the run posts. The Payroll Entry (module 3) books the month's payroll as an accrual Journal Entry: debit the expense accounts (salary expense by component, addressed by each employee's Payroll Cost Center), credit the custody payables (PAYE, pension, NHF at their withheld amounts), credit the net-pay liability (the amount owed to employees, cleared by the payment run). The employer-borne lines debit their expenses and credit their payables in the same posting.

The posting read — the one-time proof, then the monthly confirmation.

1. After the first run (module 3), open the run's accrual Journal Entry and use View > Accounting Ledger.
2. Read the rows against the wiring map above: each expense line present at the register's totals, each custody credit at the register's deduction totals, the net-pay credit at the register's net total, every P&L row carrying its cost center.
3. Any mismatch is a wiring fault — the component's Accounts row corrected, the posting corrected by the Accounts track's rules, the read repeated.
4. Thereafter the read is the payroll tie, monthly, in minutes: register column totals = posting lines = custody account movements (the General Ledger report per account) = zero after remittance. The Accounts track runs this tie from its side; this chapter is where the payroll operator makes it true from theirs.

The cost-center consequence, restated. The posting carries each employee's Payroll Cost Center onto the expense rows — which is the entire mechanism behind a true branch salary line. The module 1 walk that filled the field, and the Accounts track's unaddressed check that watches the fallback, meet here.

Practical rule: the wiring is verified before the first live run and re-verified whenever a component is added or its account row touched — one preview posting read against the map. A wrong account row mis-posts silently, every month, for every employee; the read costs ten minutes once.

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — The remittance workflow
lessons.html:
The custody accounts fill at the run and must empty at remittance. This chapter is the monthly workflow — the Accounts track's six-step filing routine, executed from the payroll chair.

The workflow, per custody, in order.

1. Close the register. The month's Salary Register (Chapter 8) produced and filed — the document-level evidence every schedule derives from.
2. Produce the schedules. From the register's export: the per-state PAYE schedule (Chapter 5), the per-PFA pension schedule with RSA numbers and both shares (Chapter 3), the NHF schedule, the levy computations. Each schedule's total is written beside its custody account's balance — they must agree, which is the payroll tie's remittance face.
3. Prepare the payments. One Payment Entry per authority per obligation: paid from the tax-reserve bank account (the Accounts track's reserve — payroll custodies are swept there at the run, per that track's schedule), debiting the custody payable, with the schedule reference in the entry and the schedule attached.
4. Release under the separation. The preparer never releases (the Accounts track's rule 1 of bank governance); the payroll operator prepares, the release authority releases.
5. File by the dates. The calendar's lines, each owned by name: PAYE to each state by its day; pension inside its days-from-salary window — the tightest line, pinned to the actual salary payment date, not the month's end; NHF and the levies per their cycles. Where a portal filing accompanies the payment, the filing is made from the schedule (one source), and the acknowledgment joins the file.
6. Verify the zero. After the cycle, each custody account's balance returns to zero (the General Ledger report per account, or the Trial Balance line). A custody that will not zero is telling one of the Accounts track's four stories — a skipped tie, a short or misposted payment, prior residue, or custody spent — and the payroll operator reads the same diagnostic from this side.

The evidence bundle. Per custody per month, one folder: the register extract, the schedule, the Payment Entry, the receipt or acknowledgment, the zero check. The certificate-and-receipt file is what answers the employee's "was my pension actually paid?" — with their PFA's schedule line and the payment's receipt, in one look — and what answers the authority's query the same way.

The penalty line. The Accounts track's rule closes this chapter unchanged: penalties on late statutory remittance are the most expensive credit line available, taken by default. The calendar with named owners, the reserve funded at the run, and the zero check every cycle are the three lines that keep the penalty figure at its target: zero, watched monthly.

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — The Salary Register
lessons.html:
Open the Salary Register report (awesome bar). One row per salary slip for the selected period and filters, with the components as columns — the month's payroll on one screen, and the source of every schedule this module produces.

The filters. Company; the period (from/to); Employee or Department where a subset is wanted; and the docstatus filter — the standing read is submitted slips only, because draft slips are computations, not payroll. Run it after every run closes (module 3), and file the month's copy in the payroll folder.

The columns and the reads. The register shows, per employee: the earnings components, the deductions components, gross, total deduction, net — plus the loan and advance columns where those features run (module 5's territory). The standing reads:

1. The column totals — the figures the whole compliance chain hangs on: total PAYE (the remittance sum before its state split), total pension by share, total NHF, gross and net. These totals are what Chapter 6's posting read ties to the Journal Entry, and what Chapter 7's schedules must sum back to.
2. The month-on-month comparison — this month's register beside last month's: the headcount delta explained by joiners and leavers (module 3's run checklist), each material per-employee movement explained by a documented event (a rise's new assignment, a proration, a variable-pay line). An unexplained movement is a finding before payday, which is the comparison's whole point.
3. The export-and-group reads — the register exported and grouped: by state of residence (Chapter 5's PAYE schedules), by PFA (Chapter 3's pension schedules), by Payroll Cost Center (the branch salary read the P&L will confirm).

The confidentiality rule. The register is the most sensitive report on the site: every salary, named. Its governance is the sysadmin track's machinery applied without exception:

• Access: the payroll operator, the release/review authority, the accountant — role-permissioned, nobody else. The HR-adjacent curiosity read is not a use case.
• Exports: each export exists for a schedule or a filing; it is stored in the payroll folder (business-controlled, per the backup-custody logic), never in personal drives or chat threads; and export permission on the payroll doctypes is part of module 2-of-sysadmin's matrix.
• The register in meetings: aggregates travel (totals, by cost center); named rows do not, outside the roles above.

Practical rule: the register is produced once per month as the closed record and every schedule derives from that one export — schedules produced from fresh ad-hoc runs at different moments are how the PAYE schedule and the pension schedule quietly disagree about the same month. One register, many derivations.

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Case study: HealthTrade's statutory build
lessons.html:
The statutory layer built onto module 1's structures, and the first full cycle run. Every chapter appears.

The slab (Chapter 2). The accountant brings the current PAYE computation sheet; the Income Tax Slab is built from it — exemption figure, band rows — named and dated, submitted, and read back against the sheet line by line before use. The PAYE component is created with the taxable-salary flag and wired to PAYE Payable; the slab attaches to all thirty assignments in one governed pass. The plausibility check runs on one Head Office slip: taxable earnings summed, walked through the accountant's paper computation — first pass disagrees by a small monthly amount, traced in twenty minutes to the Meal allowance flagged Is Tax Applicable when the ruling said exempt. The component flag is corrected, the register's ruling column updated, the check re-run: agreement to the naira. One slip's check; thirty slips inherit the fix.

Pension (Chapter 3). Pension — Employee and Pension — Employer built on (B + H + T) at the accountant's rates; the employer share configured visible-but-excluded-from-net; both wired to Pension Payable. The Employee-record walk from module 1 pays off: all thirty carry PFA and RSA numbers except one joiner — chased and captured at joining, not at remittance day. The hand-check: two multiplications on one slip, agreed.

The applicability page (Chapter 4). Written with the accountant in one sitting: NHF ruled per the current position with the covered categories conditioned on the component; NSITF ruled applicable, implemented as the accountant's monthly journal from the register totals (the one-home rule recorded); ITF ruled by the threshold and diarised on the threshold watch. Every line carries its source and date.

The wiring read (Chapter 6). Before the first live run, the preview posting is read against the map — and catches one wiring fault: NHF's account row pointed at PAYE Payable (a copy-paste at component creation). Corrected in the Accounts table, re-read, clean. The fault would have merged two custodies' balances and broken both zero checks, silently, from month one.

The first cycle (Chapters 5, 7, 8). The run closes (module 3's procedure); the Salary Register is produced once and filed. The derivations follow: the state grouping yields two PAYE schedules — Lagos and Ogun (three Ogun-resident staff the residence walk had captured); the PFA grouping yields four pension schedules; NHF's schedule lists its covered staff. Payments prepare from the reserve, release under the separation, file by the calendar — pension inside its days-from-salary window, tracked from the actual payment date. The zero check closes the cycle: PAYE Payable, Pension Payable, NHF Payable all at zero; the month's evidence bundles filed. The accountant's note in the payroll log: the register, the posting, the schedules, and the payments are one set of numbers for the first time — the tie holds at every link.

lessons.title: Chapter 10 — Common mistakes & the second law
lessons.html:
The statutory layer's recurring failures, then the review list.

Pattern 1 — the improvised rate. Symptom: a percentage typed from memory or a forum; deductions the law does not support, or shortfalls it penalises. Cause: the division of authority ignored (Chapter 1). Fix: the rule made absolute — every rate, band, and ruling enters from the accountant's current table, recorded on the register with source and date, re-read annually and at every reform.

Pattern 2 — the drifted slab. Symptom: PAYE computed on last regime's bands months after a reform; the compliance failure automated. Cause: the slab treated as set-and-forget (Chapter 2). Fix: the annual re-read on the calendar, reforms producing a new dated slab attached by new assignments, and the plausibility check re-run on one slip at every slab change.

Pattern 3 — the wrong-flag component. Symptom: the exempt allowance taxed, or the taxable one exempted — every slip wrong by the same small amount. Cause: Is Tax Applicable set by guess (Chapters 1-2). Fix: the flag ruled per component on the register, and the plausibility check — one slip against the accountant's paper computation — at build and at every flag change.

Pattern 4 — the merged custodies. Symptom: custody accounts that never zero cleanly; two obligations' money indistinguishable. Cause: Accounts-table wiring faults (Chapter 6). Fix: the wiring map verified by the posting read before the first run and at every component change — ten minutes against a silent monthly mis-post.

Pattern 5 — the from-memory remittance. Symptom: payments made without schedules; the state split guessed; the PFA schedule reconstructed when a fund queries; the register and the payments disagreeing about the same month. Cause: derivations skipped or run from ad-hoc extracts (Chapters 5, 7, 8). Fix: one monthly register as the closed record, every schedule derived from it, every payment carrying its schedule, and the zero check closing each cycle.

Pattern 6 — the leaked register. Symptom: the salary register in personal drives and chat threads; every salary effectively public. Cause: the confidentiality rule unenforced (Chapter 8). Fix: role-permissioned access, exports only for schedules and filings into the business-controlled folder, aggregates-not-names in meetings, and the export permission in the sysadmin matrix.

The review list. Before the quiz, confirm you can: state the custody frame and the division of authority; build an Income Tax Slab from the accountant's sheet, create the PAYE component with its taxable-salary flag, attach the slab on assignments, and run the plausibility check; build both pension shares on the B/H/T family with the employer share visible-but-excluded, and produce the per-PFA schedule; keep the applicability register with its annual re-read and threshold watch; maintain the state field and produce the per-state schedule; verify the wiring by the posting read and run the monthly payroll tie; execute the six-step remittance workflow with its evidence bundle and zero check; and govern the Salary Register — one monthly record, derived schedules, confidentiality enforced.

The second law: statutory amounts are computed by components from the accountant's current table, posted to typed custody accounts, remitted by the calendar from the reserve, and zeroed every cycle. Module 3 runs the payroll itself: the Payroll Entry.
